messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Vulnerability: Being naked, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Vignette:
Minh Tran was a 46-year-old married software engineer who had come to treatment after months of feeling as if a part of him was still trapped in a war zone. He grew up in a South Eastern Asian family and had built a stable life in the United States, working long hours at his computer and sharing a home with his wife. Until recently, he had seen himself as steady and private, someone who handled stress by keeping his head down and concentrating on work. That changed after his combat exposure, which he described only in fragments at first, pausing for long stretches as though the details were difficult to bring into words. What he could say was that there had been a frightening event during deployment that stayed with him in a way he could not shake, and that even now, trying to speak about it felt almost impossible. When he did try, he said the memories came back like a film he was forced to watch again and again, with no control over when it started or how long it would last.

Minh said that at times the recollection was not just visual. Certain sounds seemed to return inside his head exactly as they had during the event, especially the mechanical noise of motorcycles. He would hear that sound in ordinary life and suddenly feel pulled back into the same moment, as if the noise were arriving from very close by rather than from the street outside. The same happened with smells that reminded him of the setting in which the trauma occurred; a related odor could catch him off guard and leave him tense and disoriented before he had time to think. He noticed these reactions first in the months after returning home, when he was trying to resume normal routines and expected the disturbance to settle on its own. Instead, the memories stayed vivid and repetitive, arriving in his mind without warning and often without language. He could see and hear parts of what happened, but he could not neatly tell the story of it, and that inability frustrated him. He said it felt as if the event existed as a set of images and sounds rather than something he could place into words and leave behind.

Over time, Minh began organizing his days around avoiding anything that might set those experiences off. He stopped watching television programmes and films that involved combat, violence, or similar events, and he avoided reading news or stories that reminded him of what he had lived through. He found that going out at all had become difficult, especially to unfamiliar places where he felt unable to assess what might happen. Even a simple trip somewhere new could leave him scanning exits and entrances, feeling unable to relax. He also stopped exercising regularly, partly because physical exertion made him feel exposed and vulnerable in a way he did not want to name at first. One feeling in particular disturbed him: being naked, even briefly, left him uncomfortably aware of his vulnerability, as though he had lost the protection needed to stay safe. At home, where he had once expected to settle, he now found himself on guard inside his own walls. He described sitting in the living room and feeling as if he still needed to keep watch, listening for sounds that did not belong. His wife noticed that he had become more constrained and harder to draw into shared activities, and he himself recognized that the world had gradually shrunk to the familiar paths between home and work.

His job as a software engineer gave him a structured environment, but even there the effects were hard to ignore. He could concentrate better when he stayed seated at his desk, yet the ordinary movement of getting to and from work, or walking into an unfamiliar building, could leave him keyed up and uneasy. Outside his apartment and office, strangers approaching him in ordinary situations felt threatening in a way he knew was out of proportion to the moment, but that knowledge did not make the feeling go away. He would become alert when someone came toward him too quickly on the sidewalk or in a public place, and he found himself watching people’s hands, their distance, and their body language before they even spoke. Motorcycle noise was especially difficult in city traffic; when one passed close by, he would tense immediately, his attention narrowing as if danger might be following the sound.

Minh eventually sought help when the strain of living this way became harder to contain. He was tired of guarding himself at home, avoiding places, and arranging his life around what might remind him of the trauma. He also worried that the film-like memories, the sounds that returned in his head, and the sense that he could not put the event into words were keeping him from being fully present with his wife and from feeling settled in his own life. What he wanted most was relief from the constant state of watchfulness and the fear that something ordinary—a smell, a motorcycle, an unfamiliar street, another person approaching him—could throw him back into the same frightening moment all over again.
